_comment_family: Raleway ships as a family and the two files in fonts/ are two cuts of
it - this Regular and the Bold beside it - both carrying 'Raleway' as
name ID 1, with the cut in the subfamily. Asking for 'Raleway' alone
would let either of them answer, and these two are used TOGETHER on
one line: the Bold is what a picked word is set in, so a Regular
answering in its place would leave the highlight identical to the
words either side of it. So the full name (name ID 4) is what gets
declared, exactly as the two Telegraf packs do and for their reason.
There is a second reason here that none of those packs has, and it is
the stronger of the two: 'Raleway' is already taken inside this app.
The interface is set in it - vendor/raleway.css declares a family by
that exact name at five weights, self-hosted, and index.html loads it
before anything else. registerFace skips a face whose family is
already in document.fonts (see js/channels.js), so a pack declaring
'Raleway' would never be registered from this JSON at all: the file in
fonts/ would go unread and the canvas would quietly draw captions with
the INTERFACE webfont - a latin subset chosen for buttons and labels,
not the face a channel was measured against. Nothing would report it,
because from the browser's side a family by that name was found. A
distinct family name is what keeps the two apart.
Weight 400, which is the file's own usWeightClass and what the cut is
called. Stated rather than left to 'normal' so the pairing with the
700 next door is written down on both halves of it.
_comment_css: Not declared in styles.css: this face arrived with a channel and is
registered from this JSON, which is the route content/README.md
describes. Nothing has to be added to the stylesheet for it - and in
this one case that is a rule worth not bending, since the stylesheet
is where the interface's own Raleway comes in and a second declaration
beside it is the collision the family name above exists to avoid.
_comment_local: What the machine may already know the face by, tried after the file.
The first is the Windows full name (name ID 4) and the second the
PostScript name; both name this one cut rather than the family, so a
machine answering to either is answering with a Regular. 'Raleway' on
its own is deliberately absent: it is the name the Bold answers to as
well, and here it is also the name the interface's webfont answers to.
Worth knowing that this fallback is likelier to fire on a real machine
than most in this folder - Raleway is one of the most widely installed
faces in the world - and that what it hands back may be a different
release with different metrics. That is the usual bargain of local():
it is the route taken only when the file is gone, and a caption set in
a neighbouring version of the right typeface is a far smaller failure
than one set in a substitute.
_comment_stack: The fallbacks are damage limitation and never a design choice - a
title laid out against the wrong metrics is broken, not merely
different, which is what fontguard exists to catch before it is ever
drawn. They are still chosen rather than copied, and this face has a
first fallback nothing else here can have.
'Raleway' second is the interface's own webfont, vendored into
frontend/vendor/ and therefore present on every machine this app runs
on, with no network. It is the SAME TYPEFACE at the same weight, so a
caption that lost the file falls back to Raleway rather than to an
impression of it. That is as close as damage limitation gets, and it
is why the collision described above is worth a distinct family name
rather than being avoided by not using the face at all.
